title: Cervical vasovagal shock: A rare complication of incomplete abortion case report
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
case_prompt:
A 42-year-old woman, G3P2 at 12 weeks’ gestation, presented with a 2-day history of gradual-onset vaginal spotting and crampy lower abdominal pain radiating to her back. She reported one episode of clot passage but did not observe any products of conception and denied fever, nausea, vomiting, or presyncope.  

Her medical and surgical histories were unremarkable. On examination she was alert with a blood pressure of 110/72 mmHg, heart rate of 84 bpm, and normal other vital signs. Abdominal examination revealed mild suprapubic tenderness without guarding or rebound. Speculum examination showed a slightly open cervical os with oozing blood; no products were visible.  

Laboratory studies showed a WBC count of 4.6×10^9/L, hemoglobin 11.4 g/dL, and platelets 255×10^9/L. Transvaginal ultrasound confirmed retained products of conception within the uterine cavity.  

She was administered 600 μg sublingual misoprostol. Four hours later, her blood pressure was 78/52 mmHg and heart rate was 56 bpm, and she reported passage of additional clots. Resuscitation with 1 L normal saline via two large-bore IV lines was initiated, and a urinary catheter drained 900 mL of clear urine. Crossmatching for two units of blood was underway. Fifteen minutes later, her blood pressure fell to 62/40 mmHg with a heart rate of 51 bpm and cold extremities.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Hemorrhagic (hypovolemic) shock was considered given bleeding and hypotension — “Patients with hemorrhagic shock have obvious signs of blood loss.”  
2. Septic shock was considered because of the risk of infection in incomplete abortion — “Patients with septic abortion have signs of sepsis.”  
3. Cervical vasovagal shock was identified based on reflex bradycardia coinciding with cervical stimulation — “In our case, the hypotension and bradycardia were triggered by vagal stimulation as the products of conception passed through the cervix.”
